name: libcmark (cmark)
baseline: discount (C Markdown processor); the same table also lists commonmark.js (the CommonMark JavaScript reference implementation), Markdown.pl, marked, kramdown and others
workload: Parse and render to HTML a Markdown file built by concatenating the Pro Git first-edition sources of all localizations (11 MB in the 2015 table); time is the difference between a run on the file and a run on empty input, median of ten runs.
claimed_speedup: 2015 benchmarks.md table: cmark 0.29 s vs discount 1.85 s (about 6.4x, derived from page data), commonmark.js 2.09 s (about 7.2x, derived from page data), marked 1.99 s, Markdown.pl 2921.24 s (about 10,000x, derived from page data; README states 'cmark is 10,000 times faster than the original Markdown.pl, and on par with the very fastest available Markdown processors'). hoedown at 0.21 s was faster than cmark in the same table.
hardware: Thinkpad with Intel Core 2 Duo at 2 GHz (2015 table; exact model not given)
stars_or_usage: 2.0k stars; reference C implementation of CommonMark, wrapped by many languages
tradeoffs: Strict CommonMark only, with no Markdown extensions in the core library (tables, footnotes and similar live in separate forks); standard C99 with no external dependencies; builds with MSVC, gcc, tcc and clang; fuzzed and passes the CommonMark spec tests.
caveats: First-party numbers, tier C. The table is the July 2015 revision (commit 46f7f2c) of benchmarks.md; the current benchmarks.md (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jgm/cmark/HEAD/benchmarks.md, updated June 2021) drops discount and Markdown.pl and lists only commonmark.js 0.59 s, cmark 0.12 s (about 4.9x, derived from page data) and md4c 0.04 s, so md4c is about 3x faster than cmark on a 1106 KB input on a 2.3 GHz 8-core i9 MacBook Pro. Compiler, flags and the baselines' versions are not stated (CMakeLists defaults to a Release build); 2015 hardware is a Core 2 Duo and the discount, hoedown and Markdown.pl versions are unstated. The benchmark harness is public (make bench, bench/stats.py, progit input) but the numbers were not produced by an independent run. The repo page for jgm/cmark appears to be the same project as commonmark/cmark; the 2.0k star count and 2,666 commit count were read on the commonmark/cmark page.

name: libxlsxwriter
baseline: Python XlsxWriter (the same author's pure-Python XLSX writer, the incumbent for this task)
workload: Create one worksheet of 4,000 rows by 50 columns (alternating write_number 12345 and write_string 'Foo', no formatting) and save the .xlsx file; whole-process wall time measured with hyperfine, warmup 3.
claimed_speedup: hyperfine mean 210.9 ms for C/libxlsxwriter vs 919.1 ms for Python/XlsxWriter; the page's table gives Python as 4.36 times slower than C (919.1 / 210.9 = 4.36, derived from page data). For context, rust_xlsxwriter with zlib took 152.6 ms (C is 1.38x slower) and plain rust_xlsxwriter 240.8 ms (C is 1.14x faster).
tradeoffs: Write-only (cannot read or modify existing XLSX files); needs zlib; offers a constant_memory mode that flushes rows to temp files and writes inline strings (files can grow 20-100 percent); its own docs say it is single-threaded and 'optimized but not highly optimized'.
caveats: The only numbers found are in the sister project rust_xlsxwriter's documentation, written by the same author, so first-party and tier C. The test programs are listed on the page (C, Rust and Python sources) and hyperfine is named, but compiler, flags, CPU model and Python version are not stated. One small workload (200,000 unformatted cells); libxlsxwriter loses to rust_xlsxwriter built with its zlib feature. The libxlsxwriter repo and its docs carry no benchmark of their own (docs/src/working_with_memory.dox only says a bundled dtoa makes numeric writes 40-50 percent faster). Corroborating but indirect: the Impeller README (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/m9psy/Impeller/HEAD/README.md) reports a Cython wrapper over a modified fork of libxlsxwriter at 4.69 s vs Python XlsxWriter 18.17 s for 100,000 x 10 cells on Windows, which measures the fork, not upstream.

name: libpostal
baseline: Deepparse (GRAAL-Research neural address parser; fastText, fastText-light, BPEmb and attention variants, GPU and CPU)
workload: Parse about 183,000 multinational street addresses and report mean time per address (total time / 183,000); Deepparse run with batch sizes 1 to 512 on a GPU and on a CPU, libpostal run without batching.
claimed_speedup: libpostal about 0.00004 s per address vs Deepparse fastText about 0.0004 s (GPU, batch of more than 1; about 10x, derived from page data) and about 0.0026 s (CPU, batch of more than 1; about 65x, derived from page data); Deepparse batch-of-1 figures are 0.0023 s (GPU) and 0.0128 s (CPU), and its slowest variant, BPEmbAttention on CPU, 0.0286 s at batch 1. libpostal's own README separately says it processes 10-30k addresses per second per thread.
hardware: Linux, Python 3.11, Torch 2.0, CUDA 11.7 (run 2023-03-21); the paper snippet names an RTX 2080 GPU; the CPU model is not given on the docs page
stars_or_usage: 4.9k stars; widely bound from Python, Go, Ruby, Node and others (pypostal etc.)
tradeoffs: Needs about 1.8 GB of downloaded model data (2.2 GB for the Senzing model); no batching API; trades memory and data size for speed. README reports 99.45 percent full-parse accuracy on held-out OSM data; the README says it optimizes memory first and performance last.
caveats: Independent measurement by the Deepparse authors, who are competitors and are not the libpostal team; the table sits in Deepparse's docs (read from the repo) and is attributed in the docs to their NLP-OSS 2023 paper (arXiv 2311.11846, ACL Anthology 2023.nlposs-1.3), which was not opened (egress blocked) and is known to me only from search snippets, so peer review is taken from those snippets. Tier B because the experiment code, CPU model, libpostal build flags and how libpostal was invoked (C, or a Python binding such as pypostal) are not on the page, and the docs do not say which libpostal model was used. The libpostal row has a single number (batch of more than 1 column; RAM and batch-1 cells are N/A), so ratios against Deepparse's batch-of-1 column are not like for like. Deepparse is a neural model aimed at accuracy on noisy multinational addresses; it is not a regex baseline. The README's regex-based-parser baseline guess did not match any evidence found.
